package_info.why_malicious: The faker@6.6.6 package was intentionally sabotaged by its maintainer as a form of protestware. In this version, all original source code was removed and replaced with a single statement that throws an error immediately upon import. This deliberate action causes any project that installs or upgrades to this version to fail at runtime, resulting in a denial-of-service condition for all dependent applications and pipelines. The package is therefore malicious at the macro level due to its intentional disruption of the software supply chain.

attack_chain.action: Maintainer publishes a new major version (6.6.6) of faker with all original source code removed and replaced by code that throws an error immediately upon import.
attack_chain.leads_to: Any project that upgrades to or installs faker@6.6.6 will immediately fail at runtime due to the thrown error.

attack_chain.action: Consumers of the package experience denial of service as their applications, build pipelines, or test suites fail to start or execute.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption of development workflows and production systems that rely on faker, potentially causing widespread outages and productivity loss.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for major version updates of critical dependencies that remove all or most source code, especially if the main entry point throws an error or disables all functionality. package_info.why_malicious: The faker@6.6.6 package was intentionally sabotaged by its maintainer as a form of protestware. In this version, all original source code was removed and replaced with a single statement that throws an error immediately upon import. This deliberate action causes any project that installs or upgrades to this version to fail at runtime, resulting in a denial-of-service condition for all dependent applications and pipelines. The package is therefore malicious at the macro level due to its intentional disruption of the software supply chain.

attack_chain.action: Consumers of the package experience denial of service as their applications, build pipelines, or test suites fail to start or execute.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption of development workflows and production systems that rely on faker, potentially causing widespread outages and productivity loss.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code constructs a JSON object with a property whose value is an object that sets its 'constructor' property to [].constructor, passes it to jpv.validate() alongside a schema expecting an array, and causes the validator to incorrectly accept the object as a valid array, resulting in schema validation bypass.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it deliberately manipulates the 'constructor' property of an object to mimic an array, exploiting a weakness in the schema validation logic to bypass type checks and allow non-array data to be accepted as valid.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal schema validation should strictly differentiate between arrays and objects, using robust type checks such as Array.isArray. The actual behavior allows objects to be misclassified as arrays solely based on their 'constructor' property, violating type safety and data integrity expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of setting the 'constructor' property is extremely rare and generally discouraged, especially in data validation contexts. It may occur in advanced metaprogramming, but not in typical application or validation code.
key_indicators: Object property 'constructor' explicitly set to [].constructor
Schema validation logic relying on constructor equality instead of robust type checks

Presence of non-array objects passing array schema validation

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code immediately throws an error by invoking a function that always throws, preventing any further execution and breaking all dependent applications.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The main entry point of the package is replaced with code that unconditionally throws an error as soon as the package is imported, which is a clear sign of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A normal package should provide its documented functionality and allow consumers to use its API. Instead, this version ensures that any attempt to use the package results in an immediate and unrecoverable error, violating the trust and expectations of downstream users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A package might throw an error if a critical dependency is missing, if the environment is unsupported, or if the user is using a deprecated API. However, it is not legitimate for a widely used package to throw an error unconditionally for all consumers, as this constitutes a denial of service.
key_indicators: Main entry point (index.js) contains only an error-throwing statement
Complete removal of all functional code from the package
Error is thrown immediately upon import, with no conditional logic
No legitimate functionality or exports are provided

package_info.why_malicious: The faker@6.6.6 package was intentionally sabotaged by its maintainer as a form of protestware. In this version, all original source code was removed and replaced with a single statement that throws an error immediately upon import. This deliberate action causes any project that installs or upgrades to this version to fail at runtime, resulting in a denial-of-service condition for all dependent applications and pipelines. The package is therefore malicious at the macro level due to its intentional disruption of the software supply chain.

attack_chain.leads_to: Any project that upgrades to or installs faker@6.6.6 will immediately fail at runtime due to the thrown error.

attack_chain.action: Consumers of the package experience denial of service as their applications, build pipelines, or test suites fail to start or execute.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption of development workflows and production systems that rely on faker, potentially causing widespread outages and productivity loss.

All functional code removed in a new major version and replaced with a single error-throwing statement

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for major version updates of critical dependencies that remove all or most source code, especially if the main entry point throws an error or disables all functionality. Automated dependency analysis tools should flag packages where the main export is a function that only throws, or where the package contents are drastically reduced compared to previous versions. Review changelogs and diffs for sudden, unexplained code removal and error-throwing logic in the main entry point.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uses lodash.defaultsDeep to merge a crafted JSON object containing a constructor.prototype payload into a target object, resulting in the addition of a property ('a0') to Object.prototype, which pollutes all objects in the environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it demonstrates the ability to modify Object.prototype by merging attacker-controlled input containing 'constructor.prototype'. This can allow an attacker to inject arbitrary properties into all objects, leading to widespread application compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, object merging functions like defaultsDeep should only affect the target object and its direct properties. Modifying Object.prototype is highly unexpected and dangerous, as it changes the behavior of all objects globally.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of object merging should never result in prototype chain modification. Only very low-level framework or polyfill code might intentionally touch Object.prototype, but this is rare, discouraged, and should never occur via user input.
key_indicators: Use of 'constructor.prototype' or '__proto__' keys in input data
Modification of Object.prototype properties at runtime
No input validation or sanitization to prevent prototype pollution
Merging of untrusted or user-controlled objects using lodash.defaultsDeep

This enables property injection, code injection, or denial of service by altering the behavior of all objects in the JavaScript environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Altering a core array method to return incorrect results based on array length is deceptive and can silently break application logic. This behavior is intentionally misleading and difficult to detect during normal debugging.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Array.prototype.includes should accurately check for the presence of an element in an array. This patch introduces false negatives for arrays of odd length, violating the method's contract and causing logical errors.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for monkey-patching Array.prototype.includes to return false based on array length. Such behavior is not found in standard debugging or polyfilling scenarios.

package_info.why_malicious: Greatness is a Phishing-as-a-Service toolkit explicitly designed to facilitate credential theft by mimicking Microsoft 365 login pages, intercepting multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, and employing advanced evasion techniques such as JavaScript obfuscation, anti-bot logic, dynamic content loading, and encrypted exfiltration. Its sole purpose is to enable unauthorized access to Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing user credentials and session data.

attack_chain.action: Victim receives a phishing email or PDF containing a QR code that directs them to a malicious login page designed to mimic Microsoft 365.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim visits the phishing site.

attack_chain.action: Phishing site loads obfuscated and dynamically loaded JavaScript, implements anti-bot and CAPTCHA evasion to avoid automated detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is presented with a fake Microsoft 365 login page.

attack_chain.action: Victim enters credentials and MFA code into the fake login form, which captures and prepares the data for exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials and MFA code are captured by the phishing kit.

attack_chain.action: Captured credentials and MFA code are encrypted, packaged with a JWT, and exfiltrated to the attacker's server using AJAX POST requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives credentials and session data.

attack_chain.action: Attacker is notified via Telegram bot of new stolen credentials, enabling rapid exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker uses credentials and session cookie to access the victim's Microsoft 365 account.

behavioral_signatures: Phishing pages that closely mimic Microsoft 365 login, capturing both credentials and MFA codes
Obfuscated JavaScript with dynamic loading of additional code from non-standard or attacker-controlled domains
Use of CAPTCHA and custom anti-bot logic to evade automated security analysis and sandboxes
AJAX POST requests containing encrypted payloads (e.g., AES-encrypted JSON) sent to unknown or non-Microsoft endpoints after credential input
Outbound HTTP requests to the Telegram Bot API (api.telegram.org) containing credential data for attacker notification
file_indicators: HTML attachments or web pages with Microsoft 365 branding but source code or form actions pointing to non-Microsoft domains
PDF documents containing QR codes that resolve to suspicious or non-Microsoft URLs
JavaScript files or inline scripts with heavy obfuscation, Base64-encoded strings, or dynamic script loading from unfamiliar domains
network_indicators: AJAX or fetch requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.com, cdn.attacker.com) not associated with Microsoft
Outbound connections to api.telegram.org with embedded bot tokens and chat IDs
Dynamic script loading from domains not associated with trusted CDNs or Microsoft infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for phishing emails or PDF attachments containing QR codes that direct users to non-Microsoft login pages. Analyze web traffic for AJAX POST requests with encrypted payloads (such as AES-encrypted JSON) to unknown or suspicious domains, especially following credential or MFA input. Flag any use of the Telegram Bot API for outbound notifications from web pages, particularly when containing credential data. Detect obfuscated JavaScript and dynamic script loading from non-standard or attacker-controlled sources. Employ sandboxing and behavioral analysis to identify anti-bot and CAPTCHA evasion logic, and correlate with file and network indicators for comprehensive detection.

matched_snippet.code_snippet: fetch('https://scarf.sh/track', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ package: 'angular-calendar', ... }) })
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the code collects telemetry data including package usage and environment information, then sends this data to a remote server (scarf.sh) via HTTPS POST, resulting in potential exfiltration of user or environment data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Open source dependencies rarely collect and transmit telemetry data to external servers without explicit user consent, making this behavior unexpected and privacy-invasive.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal package usage does not involve exfiltrating usage or environment data to third parties, especially without opt-in or clear disclosure.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry is sometimes used in proprietary software or with explicit user opt-in, but is rare and controversial in open source libraries.
key_indicators: Network request to external telemetry server (scarf.sh)
Collection and transmission of environment or usage data
No opt-in or user notification for telemetry collection
Telemetry code present in a dependency rather than the main package

package_info.why_malicious: Version 5.3.5 of styled-components introduced a postinstall script (protestware) that executes arbitrary code during installation. While the specific script in this case is not overtly malicious, the addition of an install script in a widely used package is highly unusual and creates a significant risk vector, as it allows for arbitrary code execution on user systems during package installation. This behavior is rare in the npm ecosystem and is commonly exploited by malware.

attack_chain.action: User installs or updates a dependency (e.g., styled-components@5.3.5) that introduces a postinstall script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution during installation.

attack_chain.action: Telemetry-collecting dependency (e.g., @scarf/scarf via angular-calendar) is imported, sending usage data to a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential exfiltration of environment or usage data.

attack_chain.action: Native code dependency (e.g., deasync) is loaded, executing unauditable binary code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for hidden malicious payloads or privilege escalation.

attack_chain.action: Troll or parody package (e.g., bowserify) injects unwanted assets and code into application bundles.
attack_chain.leads_to: Polluted or altered application behavior, user confusion.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of install or postinstall scripts in package.json (scripts.install/postinstall) that execute external files or commands
Network requests to known telemetry or tracking domains (e.g., scarf.sh) at import-time or runtime
Loading of native binary modules (.node files) in JavaScript packages during import or execution
Injection of non-standard assets (e.g., images) or code into bundles by dependencies
Package names that closely resemble or parody popular packages (typosquatting/parody)
file_indicators: package.json with install or postinstall scripts referencing external files
node_modules/**/build/Release/*.node
node_modules/@scarf/scarf/**
node_modules/bowserify/**
Unexpected image or asset files (e.g., bowser.png) in application bundles
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS requests to scarf.sh/track
Any network request during install or import-time to unknown or unapproved domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified install/postinstall scripts in package.json during dependency updates. Flag packages that load native binaries (.node files) or make network requests at import-time or runtime. Detect dependencies that inject unexpected assets or code into application bundles. Identify package names that closely resemble popular packages (typosquats or parodies). Alert on outbound network connections to known telemetry or tracking domains from dependencies, especially during installation or import-time.
